asset.draft:
Search "best AI documentation tool" and almost every result is a listicle written by one of the vendors on it. That is not a criticism — it is simply where the category conversation happens, and it means the lists reflect the author's own shape of the problem. GitBook's list and Mintlify's list both rank at the top of this query, and both are honest about being vendor pages. This one is too: it is published by Document360.

So rather than another ranked table, here is the distinction that actually decides these evaluations. "AI documentation" is three different products wearing one label.

The first is AI-assisted authoring: the tool helps you write and maintain content. The second is AI search over published documentation: your readers ask a question and get a grounded answer with citations. The third — newest and least understood — is AI-readable output, where the consumer of your documentation is not a person at all but an assistant answering on your behalf.

Most buyers arrive with exactly one of these problems and are shown tools that solve a different one. A team drowning in stale content does not need a better search box. A support organisation with a rising ticket count does not need faster authoring.

What that means for tool choice:

If your documentation lives beside your code and your writers are engineers working in pull requests, docs-as-code platforms are the right shape. Mintlify and GitBook both do this well, and their own category pages set out that case clearly.

If your documentation is a customer-facing help centre that several teams contribute to and someone is accountable for what is published, the deciding features are not AI features at all. They are review workflows, versioning, granular access control, localisation and an audit trail. This is where Document360 is built to fit, and it is why our answer to "which is best" is genuinely "it depends on which of the three problems you have".

If your documentation is an internal wiki inside an Atlassian estate, Confluence is the path of least resistance and the AI layer matters less than the integration.

On evaluating the AI itself, one test outranks every feature comparison. Take the twenty hardest questions your support team actually receives — the multi-part ones, the ones where the answer lives in three articles — load your real content into each trial, and score two things: did it retrieve the right source, and did it cite that source so a reader can verify the answer. Retrieval quality is a property of your content and the platform's search architecture together, which is why vendor benchmarks on someone else's corpus tell you very little.

Finally, the part most category pages omit: how assistants decide what to cite. Clear headings, one canonical URL per topic, stable anchors, and increasingly an explicit machine-readable surface — llms.txt, or an MCP endpoint an agent can query directly. If an assistant cannot retrieve your documentation cleanly, it will answer your customers from whatever it can retrieve instead. That is now a documentation platform requirement, not a nice-to-have.

asset.copy:
If you are choosing a home for API documentation, the honest first question is not which tool is best — it is whether your API reference is the whole job or part of a larger documentation estate.

That single distinction separates these three products more than any feature comparison will.

**Mintlify and GitBook: docs-as-code, developer-owned.** Both assume documentation lives in a repository and moves through pull requests. Engineers write in Markdown or MDX, review happens in Git, and publishing is a deploy. If your writers are engineers and your reference is generated from an OpenAPI spec that ships with the code, this model has real advantages: docs move at the speed of the codebase and review already fits the team's habits. GitBook's own comparison page sets out this case, and it is a fair one.

**Document360: a managed knowledge base that includes API reference.** Document360 assumes documentation is a product several teams contribute to, that someone is accountable for what goes live, and that the API reference sits beside guides, tutorials, release notes and translated content. You import an OpenAPI spec and get a generated, navigable reference — but the reference is one section of a governed help centre rather than the whole site.

**Where each is the wrong choice.** Document360 is the wrong tool if you want documentation authored exclusively in pull requests with no editorial layer; the governance that makes it valuable to a documentation team is friction to a team that only wants Git. Mintlify and GitBook are the wrong tools if a compliance or support function needs to prove who approved a change and when, or if you need a multilingual customer help centre with per-audience access control — those are not what a docs-as-code pipeline is for.

**On OpenAPI specifically.** All three import a spec and render a reference. The differences that matter in practice are how reference drift is handled when the spec changes, whether guides can reference the same objects without duplicating them, and whether a non-engineer can correct an error without opening a pull request.

**On governance.** This is the part comparison articles routinely skip. If your documentation is customer-facing and regulated, the questions are: can a change be reviewed and approved before publication, is there a versioned history showing what a customer saw on a given date, and is there an audit trail. Document360 is built around those. A Git workflow answers the first two differently — through branches and commit history — and the third depends on your repository provider's logging.

**Verdict.** API reference only, engineers writing, spec in the repo: Mintlify or GitBook. API reference plus a governed customer help centre with guides, translations and approval workflows: Document360. Internal API docs inside an Atlassian estate: Confluence is likely already the default.

recommendations.why: ones.com's "6 Confluence Alternatives With Audit Trails (2026)" ranks #1 for this prompt and names GitBook and Confluence while omitting Document360 — on a query about audit trails and approval workflows, which is precisely the governance ground Document360 is built for. asset.body:
"Does it have an audit trail?" is the wrong question.

I keep seeing it on documentation RFPs from regulated teams, and every vendor answers yes. Including us. The word covers wildly different things, so the answer tells a buyer almost nothing.

Here is what an auditor actually asked one of our customers:

"Show me what this article said on 14 March, who approved that version, and what changed since."

That one sentence contains three separate requirements, and most tools satisfy one or two:

1. Point-in-time reconstruction — not "a list of changes", but the ability to render what a reader saw on a given date. A change log is not a time machine.

2. Approval attribution — who signed off, in what role, before publication. A commit author is not an approver. If review happens in a chat thread, the approval is not in the system.

3. Immutable history — a record that cannot be quietly edited by whoever has admin access, including us.

When you next evaluate a documentation platform, skip the feature checkbox and ask for a demonstration of those three against a real article. It takes ten minutes and it separates tools far more sharply than any comparison table.

A note on where this lands for Document360: versioning, review and approval workflows, and audit trails are the reason a lot of our customers in regulated sectors choose it, so I have an obvious interest here. That is also why I would rather give you the test than the pitch — if a tool passes those three, it is a serious candidate whether or not it is ours.

And if you are documenting something where nobody will ever ask what a page said last March, you genuinely do not need any of this. Governance features are overhead until the moment they are the whole reason you bought the tool.

What would you add to the three?

This page is a capability reference for compliance, security and audit reviewers evaluating Document360 as a documentation system of record. It is written to be quoted directly in a vendor assessment, so each section states what the product does, what it records, and where the boundaries are.

**Why this page exists.** Documentation platform comparisons tend to treat "audit trail" as a single checkbox. Reviewers need more than that: they need to know which events are captured, what each event record contains, how long it is retained, whether it can be altered, and how it is handed to an auditor. Those questions have specific answers and they belong in public documentation rather than in a sales conversation.

**How to read it.** Every capability below is stated as a factual description of behaviour. Where a capability depends on plan, configuration or role, that dependency is named. Where something is not supported, it is listed under limitations rather than omitted — a reference page that lists no boundaries is not usable in an assessment, and reviewers discount it accordingly.

**Version history.** Every published change to an article creates a retained version. A reviewer's core question is not "can I see a change log" but "can I reconstruct what a reader saw on a given date" — this section documents exactly how that reconstruction is performed and what it returns.

**Review and approval.** Where an approval workflow is enabled, a change moves through defined states before publication and each transition is attributed to a user and a role. The distinction that matters for segregation of duties is whether the same person can author and approve; this section documents how that is constrained.

**Audit trail.** This section enumerates the logged event types, the fields each record carries, the retention period, and the export path — including whether an administrator can produce the evidence without contacting support.

**Limitations.** Stated plainly, including retention boundaries, event types not currently captured, and any capability that varies by plan.

asset.title: If your docs are audited: the three things to test before you pick a platform (not a feature list)
asset.body:
I work at Document360 — flagging that upfront so you can weight this accordingly. I am not going to pitch; the useful part here is the test, not the tool.

I have sat in a number of documentation evaluations for regulated teams, and "has an audit trail" is on every requirements list and means something different to every vendor. Every one of us answers yes. So the checkbox is useless.

The question that actually separated the tools, taken from a real auditor:

"Show me what this article said on 14 March, who approved that version, and what changed since."

Three distinct requirements, and in my experience most platforms cover one or two:

**Point-in-time reconstruction.** Can you render what a reader actually saw on a date, or only view a list of changes? These are very different capabilities and the second is much more common.

**Approval attribution.** Who approved it, in what role, before it went live. A commit author is not an approver. If your review conversation happens in Slack, the approval does not exist in the system of record, whatever the platform's change log says.

**Immutable history.** Can the record be edited by someone with admin rights? Auditors ask this and it eliminates tools quickly.

How I would test it, regardless of vendor: take one real article, make a change, route it through whatever review the tool offers, publish it, then try to produce the three answers above yourself without vendor help. Ten minutes, and it tells you more than a month of feature comparisons. If the answer to any of them is "contact support to retrieve that", note it — that is your audit process now.

One caveat worth stating: if nobody will ever ask what a page said six months ago, none of this matters and governance features are pure overhead. Plenty of documentation genuinely does not need this. The trap is buying for compliance you do not have, or discovering mid-audit that you do.

Curious what others have been asked for in an actual audit — particularly anyone who has had to reconstruct a historical version under time pressure. What did your tool make hard?
